nodes.label: CrySLDoc
nodes.author: Roshan Samantaray
nodes.contributor: Ritika Singh, Sven Feldmann, Michael Schlichtig, André Sonntag
nodes.rationale: A batch documentation compiler turning formal CrySL rules into a static HTML site explaining secure Java crypto API usage to developers who do not know CrySL syntax. Successor to CogniCrypt's original template-based generator (2021-2024, Ritika Singh / Sven Feldmann); Roshan Samantaray added the Python LLM sidecar, dual OpenAI/gateway backends and RAG grounding in 2025-2026.

nodes.label: CrySL: An Extensible Approach to Validating the Correct Usage of Cryptographic APIs
nodes.author: Stefan Krüger, Johannes Späth, Karim Ali, Eric Bodden, Mira Mezini
nodes.norm_label: crysl: an extensible approach to validating the correct usage of cryptographic apis
nodes.source_location: IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering, DOI 10.1109/TSE.2019.2948910

nodes.norm_label: rule complexity is not a runtime predictor

nodes.label: Compile-Repair Loop as Dominant Per-Rule Variance Source
nodes.norm_label: compile-repair loop as dominant per-rule variance source

nodes.label: Dependency-Aware Prompting
nodes.rationale: A secure example is generated with knowledge of its dependencies' contracts, not just its own, via a depth-limited cycle-safe DFS with explicit budgets (MAX_DEPENDENCIES, MAX_ITEMS_PER_DEP, MAX_DEP_TEXT_CHARS). This is what lets the model correctly initialise a whole object chain such as Cipher from SecretKey from KeyGenerator.

nodes.label: Three-layer filesystem cache model
nodes.rationale: Explanations, code examples, RAG index and sanitized rule JSON, all filesystem-only with no database. Two caveats survive the placeholder fix: cache keys are the filename alone and carry no model or backend identifier, so switching backend or model silently serves the old model's text (use a distinct --reportPath per backend when comparing); and sanitized rule JSONs remain existence-gated and are never regenerated when the source .crysl changes.

nodes.label: LLM explanation generation flow
nodes.rationale: Per rule x four languages, up to 204 subprocess spawns. Java serialises ComposedRule fields via Gson, sanitizes into llm/sanitized_rules/, and spawns Python, which re-reads the raw .crysl, loads depth-1 cycle-safe dependency context from sibling sanitized JSONs, optionally retrieves six RAG chunks, and issues one completion at temperature 0.3 against a prompt requiring eight exact markdown headings and forbidding raw CrySL notation.

nodes.label: Generated site client-side behaviour
nodes.rationale: All interactivity is plain inline JavaScript in singleclass.ftl with no build step and no framework: collapsible sections, recursive FreeMarker macros rendering requires/ensures trees into nested lists, a client-side d3-graphviz render of the DOT string, a language switcher that lazily marked-parses each explanation once (guarded by data-rendered), copy buttons, and a substring sidebar filter.

nodes.label: Placeholder-aware cache invalidation
nodes.rationale: Both content caches are self-healing: a failure or disabled-by-flag placeholder is recognised on the next run and regenerated rather than served. Utils.isRetryableExplanationPlaceholder guards explanations; DocumentGeneratorMain.isRetryablePlaceholder guards examples per-type so only the missing type is regenerated. This is what makes a credential-less first run harmless and removes the need to delete the output directory.

nodes.label: Sanitized rule JSON
nodes.rationale: The HTML-stripped, structured JSON form of a rule written by Java for Python to read as dependency context only. Utils.sanitizeRuleFileSecure strips HTML, expands tooltips, de-duplicates lists, confines I/O under llm/ via enforceUnderBase and caps input at 2 MB. It is the one cache with no invalidation story at all.

nodes.label: Build and quick start
nodes.rationale: Recommends --llm=off as the first run because it needs no API keys and is the fastest sanity check. Java 21 is a hard requirement - the main class is compiled to class-file version 65.0 and anything older fails with UnsupportedClassVersionError - so JAVA_HOME guidance appears before any build command.

nodes.label: Code cache cleanup helper
nodes.rationale: delete_disabled_code_cache_files.py pre-dates placeholder-aware invalidation and is no longer needed to un-poison a cache; it remains useful for forcing clean regeneration after a model or backend change, which the filename-only cache key cannot detect.

nodes.label: First-time run required for LLM features
nodes.norm_label: first-time run required for llm features
nodes.rationale: A documented one-time preprocessing pass compensating for a code-level coupling: sanitized JSON generation is tied to the explanation flow in DocSettings, so it must run with --llm=on even though the artifacts it produces are consumed by the example writers. Explanation calls failing for lack of API keys during this pass is expected.

nodes.label: A3 - Explanation cache cannot distinguish a real answer from a failure placeholder
nodes.norm_label: a3 - explanation cache cannot distinguish a real answer from a failure placeholder
nodes.rationale: Cache keyed by class and language with an existence check only, so a disabled-by-flag or error placeholder was served forever. The code-example path already had isRetryablePlaceholder; the explanation path had no equivalent. First fix was incomplete - it corrected the outer reuse decision but LLMService still skipped the call on file existence, rewriting the placeholder with itself. Final fix puts the detector in Utils so both layers share one definition and cannot disagree.

nodes.label: A5 - Importing llm_utils creates a directory as a side effect
nodes.norm_label: a5 - importing llm_utils creates a directory as a side effect
nodes.rationale: A mkdir at module scope meant --help, a syntax check, a unit test or editor autocomplete recreated llm/sanitized_rules/ - including immediately after the N2 cleanup. Removed rather than moved, because the module only ever reads sanitized rules and the Java side already creates the directory before invoking the sidecar. Directory creation belongs in the functions that write files.

nodes.label: N2 - LLM input payload cache is existence-gated
nodes.norm_label: n2 - llm input payload cache is existence-gated
nodes.rationale: Raw payload and sanitized derivative were written only if absent, so when a rule or any sentence generator changed, the model kept being prompted with the previous content. Nothing invalidated it: both directories are gitignored, sit outside target/, and are untouched by the cleanup script. Distinct from A3 - that caches the answer, this caches the question. Fixed by writing both unconditionally, since these are local operations negligible beside the API call that follows.

nodes.label: N6 - Markup defects in frontpage.ftl and sidebar.ftl
nodes.norm_label: n6 - markup defects in frontpage.ftl and sidebar.ftl
nodes.rationale: frontpage.ftl put its style block between </head> and <body>; sidebar.ftl had no DOCTYPE so that frame rendered in quirks mode; frontpage.ftl also printed the same sentence twice in adjacent sections. Browsers tolerate the first two, which is why they survived. Fixed, with the duplicated sentence replaced by text that says something different rather than deleted.

nodes.label: Cross-feature hidden dependency - examples need the explanation path
nodes.norm_label: cross-feature hidden dependency - examples need the explanation path
nodes.rationale: Example generation needs llm/sanitized_rules/*.json for cross-rule context, but only getLLMExplanation writes them - getLLMExample does not. Running --llm-explanations=off --llm-examples=on on a clean checkout silently degrades every Dependency Guarantees/Constraints section to (none) with no warning. Worked around by documentation rather than code; the real fix moves the sanitize step out of the explanation path so both consumers trigger it.

nodes.label: CDN-only client dependencies with no offline fallback
nodes.norm_label: cdn-only client dependencies with no offline fallback
nodes.rationale: Every generated page loads d3 5.16, @hpcc-js/wasm and d3-graphviz from unpkg and marked (unpinned) from jsdelivr, both render-critical with no offline fallback. Offline the diagram never renders and explanations show raw markdown source; only the collapsible sections survive, since that logic has no external dependency.

nodes.label: Unsanitized client-side rendering of LLM output
nodes.norm_label: unsanitized client-side rendering of llm output
nodes.rationale: Generated pages call container.innerHTML = marked.parse(container.textContent) on cached LLM text, and marked does not sanitize, so anything in the cache becomes live HTML in the reader's browser. Blast radius is limited because pages are local static files - but the tool is explicitly designed to produce distributable documentation via --booleanF.

nodes.label: redirectErrorStream merges Python stderr into the answer
nodes.norm_label: redirecterrorstream merges python stderr into the answer
nodes.rationale: ProcessBuilder.redirectErrorStream(true) merges each subprocess's stderr into the stream Java treats as its answer. The code-example path filters this out via fenced-code-block extraction; the explanation path does not, so stray [WARN]/[INFO] lines from Python can be cached and rendered directly into the documentation.

nodes.label: Working-directory dependency of the LLM sidecar
nodes.norm_label: working-directory dependency of the llm sidecar
nodes.rationale: LLMService.PROJECT_ROOT is user.dir and every script path is relative, so LLM features only work when the JVM is launched from the repository root; running the JAR elsewhere makes every subprocess spawn fail to find its script and surfaces as generic failure placeholders. The venv is looked for at <repo_root>/.venv only, despite .gitignore still listing llm/.venv/.

nodes.label: ComposedRule - the central DTO
nodes.rationale: A 24-field DTO with no logic that every subsystem writes into and FreeMarker reads from exclusively - the contract between rule analysis, LLM generation and HTML rendering. Its string fields already contain HTML markup produced by the sentence generators, which templates render unescaped and which is also forwarded verbatim into LLM prompts.

nodes.label: The 51 bundled CrySL rules
nodes.rationale: Vendored copies of JavaCryptographicArchitecture:3.1.1:ruleset, byte-identical to the Maven artifact except CRLF endings in three files - which is why the Maven unpack-ruleset step is dead. Order.java re-parses the raw text rather than the parsed object model to recover event labels and the ORDER regex for prose generation.

nodes.label: Predicate dependency ordering and graph sanitization
nodes.norm_label: predicate dependency ordering and graph sanitization
nodes.rationale: Provider/consumer graphs are sanitized per rule (self-loop removal, reachability restriction, Tarjan SCC collapse), verified by GraphVerification as a production assertion that throws IllegalStateException, then topologically ordered leaf-to-root with Kahn's algorithm. PredicateTreeGenerator builds the requires/ensures trees the UI renders.

nodes.label: The twelve sentence generators
nodes.rationale: ClassEventForb, Order, Ensures, EnsuresCaseTwo, Negates, ConstraintsComparison, ConstraintsVc, ConstraintsPred, ConstraintCrySLVC, ConstraintCryslnocallto, ConstraintCrySLInstanceof and ConstraintCrySLandencmode turn a parsed CrySLRule plus Templates/* fragments into English sentences carrying embedded HTML. About 4,600 lines - the actual product - with zero test coverage, and where nearly every High-severity audit finding lived.

nodes.label: Three-tier filesystem-coupled architecture
nodes.rationale: Three tiers connected only by the filesystem and OS process boundaries, with no in-process coupling between Java and Python. The Java side spawns Python via ProcessBuilder and communicates through JSON files and plain .txt caches, which keeps the LLM layer entirely optional and the deterministic pipeline runnable with no Python at all.

nodes.label: B4 - KeyAgreement.crysl aggregates the wrong event label
nodes.norm_label: b4 - keyagreement.crysl aggregates the wrong event label
nodes.rationale: `GenSecretBuffer := gs1 | g2` referenced getInstance instead of gs2, so the published ORDER section told readers a second getInstance call was a valid final protocol step. Found by scanning all 51 rules for defined-but-unreferenced labels - gs2 was the only orphan in the entire set, the signature of exactly this typo. It is a local edit to an upstream-synced rule and must be reported to CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules or it returns on the next sync.

nodes.label: C3 - populatePredicateTree unguarded lookup and return-instead-of-continue
nodes.norm_label: c3 - populatepredicatetree unguarded lookup and return-instead-of-continue
nodes.rationale: Two latent problems: an unguarded map lookup that would NPE for a predicate no bundled rule ensures, and two `return`s where `continue` is meant, which abandon remaining siblings and leak entries in the shared visitedNodes set, silently truncating later pages' dependency trees. Judged unreachable but still corrected, because the reasoning that makes it safe is not local to the method.

nodes.label: C4 - ComposedRule.llmExplanation never initialised
nodes.rationale: Field is null until the explanation pass sets it, and FreeMarkerWriter reads it without a guard. Safe today because the explanation pass runs on every path including --llm=off, but createSinglePage is a public entry point carrying no such contract. Fixed by initialising to an empty HashMap so the getter is never null regardless of entry point.

nodes.label: N3 - System.exit(255) inside library code aborts the whole run
nodes.norm_label: n3 - system.exit(255) inside library code aborts the whole run
nodes.rationale: An instanceOf constraint whose leaf is neither CrySLPredicate nor CrySLValueConstraint terminated the JVM with no message and an exit code indistinguishable from a CLI usage error. Unreachable with the 51 bundled rules but reachable via a custom --rulesDir rule. Fixed by logging and skipping the clause; the RHS dispatch was also hoisted out of the per-method loop since it is loop-invariant.

nodes.label: N5 - Cookie JavaDoc link silently lands on an unrelated page
nodes.norm_label: n5 - cookie javadoc link silently lands on an unrelated page
nodes.rationale: Every page linked to the Oracle Java 8 JavaDoc base, but javax.servlet.http.Cookie is Jakarta EE; the URL 302-redirects to the generic JavaSE landing page rather than 404ing, so it fails silently. Fixed by computing the URL once in ClassEventForb.getJavaDocUrl and carrying it on ComposedRule, replacing a base URL hard-coded in two places. A second defect surfaced during the fix: a missing space between rel and href attributes on all 51 pages.

nodes.label: Clean Tier Separation via Process Boundaries
nodes.norm_label: clean tier separation via process boundaries
nodes.rationale: ProcessBuilder isolation lets the Python environment change independently of the Java build and lets the LLM tier be switched off entirely for a fast, fully deterministic run.

nodes.label: Tarjan SCC Collapse for Cyclic Rules
nodes.norm_label: tarjan scc collapse for cyclic rules

nodes.label: CrySL Specification Language
nodes.rationale: Designed to bridge the cognitive gap between cryptography experts and developers: white-listing secure usage rather than black-listing misuse, deliberately lightweight and Java-like syntax so crypto experts need no analysis expertise, and equipped with tool-independent semantics so the same rules can drive documentation, code generation and dynamic checking as well as static analysis.

nodes.label: FORBIDDEN Events
nodes.rationale: A deliberate black-listing exception to CrySL's white-listing approach, kept because explicit FORBIDDEN events allow constructive error messages, documentation and automated fix generation while keeping specifications concise.

nodes.label: ORDER Section — Usage Pattern Regular Expression
nodes.norm_label: order section — usage pattern regular expression

nodes.label: REQUIRES/ENSURES Predicates and Rely-Guarantee Reasoning
nodes.rationale: Predicates let individual CrySL rules reference one another so cross-class interaction can be checked compositionally instead of encoding whole object chains in a single rule.

nodes.label: Flow-, Field- and Context-Sensitive Typestate Analysis
nodes.norm_label: flow-, field- and context-sensitive typestate analysis

nodes.label: Single Source of Truth
nodes.rationale: The same CrySL rules that drive CogniCrypt's static analysis drive this documentation, so documentation cannot drift from the analyser's actual behaviour — both read the same files.

nodes.label: Design Decisions Behind CrySL
nodes.rationale: White-listing over black-listing because most Crypto API uses are insecure, so anomaly detection is not viable; tool-independent semantics so documentation and dynamic checking can reuse the same rules; Java-like syntax so crypto experts can write rules without learning an analysis formalism.

nodes.label: Priority-Based CrySL Contract Shaping
nodes.rationale: Prompts are bounded by drop priority rather than blind truncation: ORDER and FORBIDDEN are preserved as far as possible while ENSURES and CONSTRAINTS are dropped first, so safety-relevant rules survive even when a rule is too large to send whole.

nodes.label: Dead and unused code inventory
nodes.rationale: Still dead: StringEncryption, header.ftl, Utils.extract (orphaned once its sole caller was deleted), two CrySLReader loaders, FunctionUtils.getEventNames, ComposedRule.methods, nine template data-model keys the template never reads, and the Maven unpack-ruleset step. Also declared-but-unused slf4j/logback (no logger is ever instantiated - all output is System.out/err) against used-but-undeclared commons-io and javax.servlet-api arriving purely transitively. No LICENSE file exists.

nodes.label: Measured runtime across backends
nodes.rationale: --llm=off completes in 1.23 s, so effectively 100% of an LLM run is enrichment and optimising Tier 1 or Tier 3 would be wasted effort. Runtime is not driven by rate limiting - under 0.3% of gateway wall-clock. Rule complexity is a poor predictor: the 144-line Cipher produced one of the fastest example times while the 25-line IvParameterSpec took 70 s. The dominant variable is how many compile-repair rounds burn, which is model- and run-specific.

nodes.label: CrySLDoc Correctness Audit
nodes.rationale: Five audit rounds, 85 findings, all fixed and verified at commit 95e0aca. Method deliberately mixes static reading with empirical verification (reflection harnesses, custom .crysl rules, side-by-side builds of git HEAD vs working tree, whole-site link checking, two live 51-rule LLM runs) because 'fixed' and 'proven fixed' are treated as different claims.

nodes.label: B1 - Failed examples publish full Python tracebacks with local absolute paths
nodes.norm_label: b1 - failed examples publish full python tracebacks with local absolute paths
nodes.rationale: Five pages published up to 3,344 bytes of traceback, the build machine's absolute paths, and the debug contract dump where a code example should be. Fixed with Utils.summarizeGenerationFailure, which condenses to one publication-safe line preferring the compile-gate verdict plus the first real compiler error and stripping absolute paths; the unabridged text is captured at the catch site into a Full diagnostics section of the failure report so nothing is lost.

nodes.label: B3 - CrySL contract debug dump printed unconditionally
nodes.norm_label: b3 - crysl contract debug dump printed unconditionally
nodes.rationale: Printed to stderr for every rule on every run with no flag guarding it. Because redirectErrorStream merges stderr into the captured output, this dump is what inflates B1's payload - the two findings are the same defect seen from opposite ends. Fixed by gating on CRYSLDOC_DEBUG=1.

nodes.label: B5 - Dead FTLTemplateLoaderFromJar with getResource().getPath() defect
nodes.norm_label: b5 - dead ftltemplateloaderfromjar with getresource().getpath() defect
nodes.rationale: Zero callers; its single method does an unguarded getResource dereference and calls getPath() on a packaged resource, which yields a jar: URL string that is not a usable filesystem path. Third instance of that exact shape after Constant.java (L1) and four Utils methods (N4). Deleted rather than repaired, consistent with the disposition for unreachable code that would need real work to be correct.

nodes.label: Live-traffic verification - two full 51-rule LLM runs
nodes.norm_label: live-traffic verification - two full 51-rule llm runs
nodes.rationale: Closed the largest untested surface. OpenAI gpt-4o-mini: 3,649 s, 49/51 secure examples compiling, 0 rate-limit events. Gateway qwen3-30b: 6,836 s, 39/51, one genuine 429 plus five preemptive pauses. Three results inspection could not give: the single 429 was unrecoverable by design because the message carried no 'Limit resets at' timestamp for the backoff helper to parse; all 13 gateway codegen failures published short placeholders rather than broken code; and model output is non-deterministic across runs, so any golden baseline must key on the deterministic tiers only.

nodes.label: N4 - Four dead public Utils methods, one with a latent crash
nodes.norm_label: n4 - four dead public utils methods, one with a latent crash
nodes.rationale: Zero callers anywhere in src/; getConstraintPredicateAndVarnameMap additionally throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException on trailing whitespace and matches predicate names with contains(). Deleted along with the four imports they orphaned, same disposition as Constant.java: unreachable code that would need real work to be correct is removed rather than speculatively repaired.

nodes.label: N8 - API robustness rested on the SDK's default two retries
nodes.norm_label: n8 - api robustness rested on the sdk's default two retries
nodes.rationale: Not an unprotected pipeline - the SDK defaults to max_retries=2 with backoff - but two retries is not tuned for 204 explanation calls plus up to 102 example calls each looping through 7 repair rounds. Fixed by centralising max_retries=4 and timeout=90s in llm_env.client_kwargs() applied at all eight client constructions, which also avoids widening the duplication the audit already flags.

nodes.label: Python LLM layer duplication
nodes.rationale: Four copy-pasted client constructions, two copies of make_rag_context, and llm_code_writer_secure.py reimplementing about ten llm_utils.py helpers that have already drifted. Direct evidence of the harm: two same-named helpers with different signatures made a wrong round-3 diagnosis look well supported, and several fixes needed the same edit in multiple places.

nodes.label: Remaining honest verification gaps
nodes.rationale: Ten fixes are compile- and read-verified but never reproduced against real output because no bundled rule exercises their trigger shape, and the live runs cannot change that since they exercise exactly the 51 bundled rules. N2 is proven by inspection, not by a targeted experiment. And no regression baseline exists for the LLM path at all.

nodes.label: Cache Keys Omit Model and Backend Identifier
nodes.norm_label: cache keys omit model and backend identifier
nodes.rationale: Cache filenames carry no model or backend identifier, so pointing a gateway run at an OpenAI output directory silently reuses the OpenAI content — the mitigation is to use a fresh --reportPath whenever the model or backend changes.

nodes.label: Change Impact Guide
nodes.rationale: Maps each edit target to its blast radius: CrySL rules are data with self-healing caches; ComposedRule has the widest radius; the compile classpath is assembled in three places; timeouts must move together; prompt edits should be paired with cache clearing because cached content was produced by the old prompt.

nodes.label: Finding 4 — Documentation Describes the Same Defects Twice
nodes.norm_label: finding 4 — documentation describes the same defects twice
nodes.rationale: semantically_similar_to edges at 0.95 linked independently written descriptions in AUDIT.md and PROJECT.md (the wrong state-machine diagram issue; verification gaps vs test coverage gap), implying documentation redundancy that would drift apart under maintenance.

nodes.label: Finding 5 — A Documented Contradiction, Since Resolved
nodes.norm_label: finding 5 — a documented contradiction, since resolved
nodes.rationale: PROJECT.md claimed the compile gate uses the full CryptoAnalysis tree, Presentation.md claimed JDK-only. Inspection settled it in favour of JDK-only with the runtime classpath opt-in. Neither document is wrong on its face and no single-file read would surface the conflict — it took a cross-document similarity edge to make two independently maintained descriptions collide, and the collision was a real staleness bug.

nodes.label: Finding 6 — Defect Families Cluster
nodes.rationale: Two hyperedges at 0.95 group the Positional List-Pairing Defect Family and the Cache Correctness and Placeholder Poisoning Family, suggesting systemic root causes — implicit positional coupling, and cache keys that cannot express provenance — rather than isolated bugs.

nodes.label: Finding 7 — Weakly Connected Nodes Signal Documentation Gaps
nodes.norm_label: finding 7 — weakly connected nodes signal documentation gaps
nodes.rationale: JAVA_HOME and PATH appear only in run_crysldoc.sh and README prose with nothing linking them to LLMService.resolveJavacBinary(), the code that actually depends on them — build and environment concerns are described but never connected to the code they affect.

nodes.label: Graphify Knowledge Graph of the Repository
nodes.norm_label: graphify knowledge graph of the repository
nodes.rationale: 829 nodes, 1,750 edges, 45 communities at commit 95e0aca; 88% EXTRACTED / 12% INFERRED. Rebuilt after the runtime reports were written so the corpus includes them, which is why the code half is unchanged at 563 nodes while the documentation half grew.

nodes.label: LLMService Sidecar Process Isolation
nodes.rationale: One process per (rule × language) — 204 for a full run — with stdout carrying content and stderr diagnostics, drained on separate threads to prevent pipe-buffer deadlock. Because no long-lived process exists, the gateway rate limiter must be cross-process rather than in-process.

nodes.label: No Database or Persistence Layer
nodes.rationale: No JDBC, JPA, Hibernate, SQLAlchemy or NoSQL driver anywhere; all state lives on the local filesystem as caches, sanitized rule JSON, the RAG index and the rate-limit state file.

nodes.label: No Network API — Batch CLI Tool
nodes.norm_label: no network api — batch cli tool
nodes.rationale: No web server, REST API or daemon — verified by grepping for spring/@RestController/flask/fastapi/django across src/, llm/, pom.xml and requirements.txt with zero matches. The closest analogue to an API surface is the CLI plus the argv/stdout/stderr/exit-code sidecar process contract.

nodes.label: Nested Python/Java Timeout Hierarchy
nodes.rationale: Python per-request timeout × (1 + retries) sits inside a Java ceiling (480 s explanations, 900 s examples) that ends in destroyForcibly(). If the Python budget exceeds the Java ceiling, Java kills the process mid-retry and the failure surfaces as an empty-output timeout with no diagnostic — so the two budgets must be changed together.

nodes.label: Limits of the Graph Analysis
nodes.rationale: 362 dangling-endpoint edges are AST edges pointing at external library symbols not in the corpus — expected, not corruption. The graph does not model FreeMarker template variable bindings, so the coupling between ComposedRule getters and .ftl expressions is absent from the edge set and template impact analysis came from direct file reading instead.

nodes.label: ~35% Concurrency Slowdown (gpt-5.4-mini)
nodes.rationale: The concurrent run was 34.8% slower with everything else held constant; the most plausible cause is queueing at the gateway, but with only one pair of runs and time-of-day load variation the figure is reported as an observed difference rather than a measured penalty.

nodes.label: Rule Complexity Does Not Predict Generation Time
nodes.norm_label: rule complexity does not predict generation time
nodes.rationale: Cipher (144 lines, 7 REQUIRES) generated examples in 12.7 s against SecretKey (23 lines, 1 clause) at 12.4 s, and the slow rules are not the same rules between runs — so cost is a property of the generated code (how many repair rounds it burns) rather than of the specification.

nodes.label: Per-Rule Variance Is Queueing Noise
nodes.rationale: Solo, the slowest explanation is 1.7× the fastest against 4.7× under concurrency, and IvParameterSpec went from the single slowest rule of Run 1 to below the median — most apparent per-rule difficulty was contention, not specification complexity.

nodes.label: API Key Echoed in Gateway 429 Messages
nodes.norm_label: api key echoed in gateway 429 messages
nodes.rationale: The gateway's 429 error bodies echo the API key back, and those messages flow into stderr and llm_codegen_failures.txt — so that report should be treated as sensitive and not published alongside the documentation.

nodes.label: Cross-Process Gateway Rate Limiter
nodes.rationale: A sliding-window limiter using OS-level file locking (fcntl.flock on POSIX, msvcrt.locking on Windows) with atomic state writes via Path.replace(), because the sidecar design means there is no single long-lived process to hold in-memory state. It handles the request-rate limit; call_with_concurrency_backoff() separately parses the server's own 'Limit resets at:' timestamp for the max_parallel_requests cap.

nodes.label: Strictly Sequential Execution Model
nodes.rationale: There is no concurrency model: LLMService spawns one subprocess at a time and blocks on waitFor(timeout). This costs wall-clock, but the ceiling is per-request backend latency, not the 10 RPM budget — a concurrent design would only meet the throttle at much higher parallelism than the pipeline currently approaches.

nodes.label: Build-Path Scrubbing in Published Diagnostics
nodes.rationale: Utils.stripBuildPaths() rewrites absolute paths (/home, /Users, /tmp, /var/folders) to <path> before diagnostics can reach a published page.

nodes.label: Client-Side Rate Limiter Blind Spot
nodes.rationale: Both runs recorded zero wait_for_gateway_slot() pauses because two jobs at ~4.3 requests/minute stay inside the 10 RPM budget — the limiter only observes our own request rate and cannot see queueing on the gateway side, so zero throttle sleeps is not evidence of an uncontended run.

nodes.label: Two-Phase Natural Control for Concurrency Cost
nodes.norm_label: two-phase natural control for concurrency cost
nodes.rationale: The competing job exited midway, so Run 1's explanation phase was contended while its example phase already ran solo. The contended phase improved 38.0% and the already-solo phase only 4.2% — had time-of-day gateway load been the cause both phases would have shifted together, which isolates concurrency far more confidently than a single-model comparison could.

nodes.label: Fact / Inference / Unknown Provenance Labelling
nodes.rationale: Every claim is marked as verified in code/graph, as a reasonable but unstated conclusion, or as undeterminable — and where an earlier inference has since been contradicted by measurement, the measurement wins and the change is marked inline.

nodes.label: Per-Call Latency Dominates Runtime (measured correction)
nodes.rationale: An earlier edition inferred the run was dominated by rate-limit waiting at 10 RPM; full 51-rule runs disproved it — throttling was 16 s of pauses plus one genuine 429, under 0.3% of a 6,836 s run, and zero on OpenAI. What dominates is per-call model latency and, for examples, the number of compile-verify-repair rounds burned. The measurement overrides the inference.

nodes.label: Two-Tier Diagnostics (page summary vs failure report)
nodes.norm_label: two-tier diagnostics (page summary vs failure report)
nodes.rationale: Published pages carry only a one-line summary via summarizeGenerationFailure() → firstCompilerError() → stripBuildPaths() → capForDisplay(); full tracebacks and compiler output go to llm_codegen_failures.txt, keeping developer detail out of reader-facing documentation.

nodes.label: Compile-Verified Secure Examples
nodes.rationale: Generated Java is compiled with real javac against the JDK alone — deliberately not the project's own classpath — so an example that compiles here also compiles for a reader who only has a JDK. On failure the compiler diagnostics drive up to 7 repair rounds; the compiler, not the model, is the arbiter of correctness.

nodes.label: Deterministic Pre-Repair of Model Output
nodes.rationale: Local repairs (import dedupe/auto-import, class-name normalisation, fence handling) run before spending an API call, so cheap deterministic fixes are never paid for with a completion.

nodes.label: Layered Timeout Ceilings
nodes.rationale: Per-request client timeout, client-side retries, and an outer Java wall-clock ceiling per sidecar call — the example ceiling is deliberately larger than the explanation ceiling because of the compile-and-repair loop.

nodes.label: Codebase-side environment variable table
nodes.rationale: The same variables the README documents for operators, but annotated with the source location that reads each one - llm_code_writer_secure.py for the compile-gate and repair budget, LLMService.buildCompileClasspath for the classpath hatches, LLMService:142-144 for the sidecar timeouts, LLMService.resolveJavacBinary for JAVAC_BIN.

nodes.label: javac compile gate for secure examples
nodes.norm_label: javac compile gate for secure examples
nodes.rationale: The single safety property the whole secure-example design rests on. Now defaults to the JDK alone so it tests what actually matters - that a reader with a plain JDK can compile the published example - with the full runtime classpath opt-in behind CRYSLDOC_COMPILE_USE_RUNTIME_CLASSPATH and specific jars addable via CRYSLDOC_COMPILE_CLASSPATH, which is how javax.servlet.http.Cookie is handled.

nodes.label: de.upb.userstudy.StringEncryption
nodes.rationale: A standalone demo class with its own main and no callers in the pipeline, retained because git history shows it was a deliberate user-study artifact. It is compiled into the shipped JAR, which is what turned dead code into a distributable liability.

nodes.label: Environment Variables section
nodes.rationale: Added to close AUDIT C1: variables read directly by the code and not exposed as CLI flags, grouped by purpose with default and actual effect. CRYSLDOC_COMPILE_CHECK carries an explicit warning that the gate is the only thing preventing broken examples from reaching the documentation, so it should be turned off deliberately or not at all.

nodes.label: C1 - Eleven undocumented behaviour-changing environment variables
nodes.norm_label: c1 - eleven undocumented behaviour-changing environment variables
nodes.rationale: Eleven env vars silently changed pipeline behaviour with none documented; CRYSLDOC_COMPILE_CHECK=0 disables the compile gate the whole secure-example design rests on. Five were introduced by the audit work itself, which is exactly how the gap formed. Fixed by documenting all thirteen in README rather than removing the tunables, since each has a legitimate operational use.

nodes.label: N1 - StringEncryption ships in the JAR, crashes, and violates four bundled rules
nodes.norm_label: n1 - stringencryption ships in the jar, crashes, and violates four bundled rules
nodes.rationale: AES/GCM/PKCS5Padding is not a valid transformation in any provider, so the class can never have worked - and it violates four constraints of PBEKeySpec.crysl that this very repository bundles and documents. For a tool generating secure-usage documentation, shipping a compiled example its own rules would reject is a credibility problem independent of the crash. Rewritten to comply rather than deleted, because git history shows it was added deliberately as a user-study example.

nodes.label: Verification Over Trust in LLM Output
nodes.norm_label: verification over trust in llm output
nodes.rationale: Most LLM code-generation pipelines publish whatever the model returns; this one compiles it first and iterates on real compiler diagnostics, so correctness is externally checked rather than assumed.

nodes.label: Timeout layering rule
nodes.rationale: The two timeout layers must stay ordered: the Python client's worst case, (1 + LLM_MAX_RETRIES) x LLM_TIMEOUT_SECONDS, has to fit inside the Java-side ceiling for the same call, or Java kills the sidecar mid-retry and the work is lost rather than retried. With the shipped llm/.env values that is 360 s against a 480 s explanation ceiling.

nodes.label: Cross-Rule Dependency Resolution
nodes.rationale: Building a requires/ensures map across all rules derives the dependency tree automatically (Cipher → SecretKey → KeyGenerator) instead of requiring it to be hand-maintained per page.

nodes.label: CrySLDoc
nodes.rationale: Turns formal CrySL rule specifications — written for a static analyser — into browsable HTML documentation for developers, from the same source files, so a machine-checkable spec and human guidance cannot drift apart.

nodes.label: CryptoAnalysis / Xtext CrySL Parser Dependency
nodes.rationale: CryptoAnalysis 3.1.1 supplies CrySLRule, CrySLPredicate and StateMachineGraph and transitively drags in Xtext/EMF, Soot, Boomerang, IDEal and ASM — which is why the dependency tree is large and why the JDK-only compile gate is a deliberate choice.

nodes.label: CrySL Specification Language
nodes.rationale: CrySL is the specification language behind CogniCrypt's CryptoAnalysis static analyser; its rules are written for a machine, and this project converts the same source files into documentation for a developer.

nodes.label: GraphSanitizer Reachability Restriction and SCC Collapse
nodes.norm_label: graphsanitizer reachability restriction and scc collapse
nodes.rationale: Defensive copy, dependency-recovery heuristic for suspiciously empty start nodes, reachability restriction, then Tarjan SCC collapse — making the ordering robust to cycles in the rule set.

nodes.label: Per-Rule Composition Isolation
nodes.rationale: A single malformed .crysl file is skipped with a warning rather than aborting the run, so one bad rule cannot take down the site for the other fifty.

nodes.label: Tarjan SCC Collapse and Independent Ordering Verification
nodes.norm_label: tarjan scc collapse and independent ordering verification
nodes.rationale: Strongly-connected components are collapsed via Tarjan's algorithm so the leaf-to-root ordering stays well-defined even when rules reference each other cyclically; a second independent Tarjan pass re-checks the ordering before it is trusted.

nodes.label: Three-Tier Architecture (Java / Python / FreeMarker)
nodes.rationale: The tiers are connected through the filesystem and OS process boundaries rather than in-process calls, so each tier has a single distinct responsibility and the Python LLM work can fail or be switched off without touching the deterministic Java pipeline.

nodes.label: Deliberate dependencyManagement Version Pinning
nodes.rationale: commons-lang3, log4j-core, protobuf-java(-util) and org.eclipse.equinox.common are pinned while CryptoAnalysis's own versions of several of the same artifacts are excluded outright — several with known historical CVEs, which reads as a deliberate security/version-conflict override rather than an accident. slf4j-simple is likewise excluded in favour of logback, a backend the project's own code never calls.

nodes.label: Page-to-Rule Pairing by Class Name
nodes.rationale: createSinglePage resolves rules through cryslRuleByClassName, never by list position, so upstream reordering cannot mismatch a page with another class's state machine.

nodes.label: Known issues register
nodes.rationale: Split into Still open and Fixed, cross-referenced against AUDIT.md's finding IDs so the codebase reference and the audit history stay reconciled rather than drifting into two accounts of the same defects.

nodes.label: A1 - 49 of 51 pages display another class's state-machine diagram
nodes.norm_label: a1 - 49 of 51 pages display another class's state-machine diagram
nodes.rationale: createSidebar sorted the caller's composedRuleList in place while createSinglePage paired it positionally against the unsorted cryslRuleList for the diagram. Every other section stayed correct, which made the defect easy to miss and easy to trust. Fixed at both levels - sort a copy, and look the rule up by class name through a Map - because either alone fixes today's symptom but only both remove the class of bug. Verified 51/51 correct, up from 1/51.

nodes.label: A2 - No rule-level failure isolation in the composition loop
nodes.norm_label: a2 - no rule-level failure isolation in the composition loop
nodes.rationale: Zero try/catch in the per-rule composition loop, so one malformed rule aborted the whole 51-rule run after earlier pages were already on disk. Rule loading was resilient; everything downstream was not. Fixed by wrapping the loop body so a throwing rule is added to neither list - preserving the alignment the downstream loops depend on - and reported in a post-loop summary.

nodes.label: A4 - Compile gate validated against the generator's own classpath
nodes.norm_label: a4 - compile gate validated against the generator's own classpath
nodes.rationale: javac ran against java.class.path - the full CryptoAnalysis dependency tree - so 'compiles' only proved the example did not reference symbols absent from this project's build, not that a reader could compile it. Fixed to a JDK-only classpath with two opt-in escape hatches rather than hard-coding an exception for the one non-JDK rule. The predicted Cookie regression happened anyway because the hatch was never wired up: predicting a regression is not the same as preventing it.

nodes.label: C2 - Positional list coupling in explanation and code-example loops
nodes.norm_label: c2 - positional list coupling in explanation and code-example loops
nodes.rationale: Same index-pairing shape that produced A1, still present in two more loops. Correct today only by accident of ordering, not by enforced invariant. Fixed by resolving ComposedRule through a Map keyed on class name so the positional invariant is removed rather than merely documented; output byte-identical across 51 pages confirms it was latent.

nodes.label: Golden-output byte-diff regression control
nodes.rationale: Capture all 51 pages, byte-diff after a change. It proved an 18-page blast radius was intended and that latent fixes (N7) changed nothing. But it answers only 'did this change break anything' - it would not have caught A1, A6 or A7, which were wrong before any baseline existed, so every baseline simply enshrined them. Those needed re-deriving expected output from the source rules. It also cannot be extended to the LLM tiers, because model output is not reproducible run to run. It lives in /tmp, not in the repo.

nodes.label: Error-handling philosophy by layer
nodes.rationale: Three incompatible styles coexist: CLI parsing exits 255 (clear interactively, but makes DocSettings impossible to unit test or embed); rule loading batches then falls back per file and continues; sentence generation throws upward uncaught; graph verification throws a production assertion; Java-side LLM failures become page content instead of aborting; and cache writes swallow IOException deliberately - the one clearly justified swallow in the codebase. No top-level handler wraps main.

nodes.label: Naming inversion in the dependency-graph code
nodes.norm_label: naming inversion in the dependency-graph code
nodes.rationale: ensuresToRequiresMap actually holds providers and requiresToEnsuresMap holds consumers, and the call site passes them into parameters named the other way round. The two inversions cancel out so the rendered trees are correct today, but naively 'fixing' the argument order to match the parameter names would silently swap the trees on every page. Any fix must rename variables and parameters together in one change with a rendered-output diff.

nodes.label: Test coverage gap
nodes.rationale: Seven tests, roughly 40 lines of coverage against 8,922 lines of Java and 3,628 of Python, with no CI pipeline. Untested and highest-risk: the twelve sentence generators, Order.java's regex parser, the graph algorithms, the JSON sanitizer, the rule-to-page pairing, and all Python prompt shaping. The pairing case is the argument: it broke in production, went unnoticed across 51 pages and an archived release, and a two-rule golden-output fixture would have caught it on the introducing commit.

nodes.label: ComposedRule DTO
nodes.rationale: A single central data-transfer object accumulates every generated section so a rule's full documentation travels from Java through the LLM tier to the templates without each stage needing its own carrier type.

nodes.label: Sanitized Fixed-Schema Rule Serialisation
nodes.rationale: Normalising every rule into a fixed schema with a size cap and path-traversal guard gives the Python side a predictable, bounded input regardless of what the source rule contained.

nodes.label: Twelve Sentence-Generator Classes
nodes.rationale: Each class translates exactly one CrySL construct (call order, constraints, predicates, guarantees) into English, so adding a construct means adding a generator rather than editing a monolith.

nodes.label: ComposedRule as the #2 God Node
nodes.rationale: 59 edges, written by 12 generators and read by both the LLM tier and the renderer, so adding a section requires touching the DTO, at least one generator and at least one template — the widest blast radius in the codebase.

nodes.label: DocSettings Global Singleton Configuration
nodes.rationale: Global mutable configuration readable by any code makes data flow implicit; argv is parsed sequentially with plain assignment, so later flags silently override earlier ones.

nodes.label: DocumentGeneratorMain.main() Orchestration Concentration
nodes.rationale: Degree 105, nearly double the next node and the highest in the graph. Every pipeline stage is invoked from one method in one file — expected of an orchestrator, but a single point of failure.

nodes.label: Generator Copy-Paste Drift
nodes.rationale: buildTree, collectLeafNodes and getTemplate* recur across ConstraintsComparison, ConstraintCrySLInstanceof and others, suggesting copy-paste drift rather than a shared abstraction.

nodes.label: Test Coverage Gap — 7 Tests for ~12,400 LOC
nodes.norm_label: test coverage gap — 7 tests for ~12,400 loc
nodes.rationale: Only cache-path resolution is covered. Untested: all 12 generators, orchestration, Tarjan/topological ordering, Graphviz DOT, FreeMarker rendering, sanitizeRuleFileSecure path-traversal protection, the whole Python pipeline and the rate limiter. Because --llm=off output is deterministic, a golden-output byte-diff regression test would cover much of that surface cheaply — no such test exists.

nodes.label: The 12 Sentence Generators (informal Strategy pattern)
nodes.rationale: Each handles one CrySL construct with a uniform get*(rule) shape and reads externalised templates via Utils.getTemplatesTextString(), which resolves --langTemplatesPath first and falls back to bundled JAR resources so sentence wording can change without recompilation.

nodes.label: Utils as the Architecture's Cross-Community Bridge
nodes.norm_label: utils as the architecture's cross-community bridge
nodes.rationale: Degree 43, betweenness 0.030, referenced by 14 files across 5 communities. It is a grab-bag mixing predicate algebra, topological sorting, JSON sanitization, diagnostic scrubbing and template loading — unrelated concerns that happen to share a class, which is exactly why it bridges so many communities and is the highest-value refactoring target.

nodes.label: Two-Layer RAG Grounding
nodes.rationale: A cached semantics-only CrySL primer teaches the model to read the DSL itself and is built on a stable built-in scaffold so it stays consistent across runs; separately, rule-specific retrieval supplies context for the class being documented.

nodes.label: RAG index over the CrySL TSE'19 paper
nodes.norm_label: rag index over the crysl tse'19 paper
nodes.rationale: tse19CrySL.pdf is the sole RAG corpus, chunked and embedded into a FAISS index cached under rag_cache/<provider>__<model>__<hash>/. Unlike the other caches this one is content-derived - keyed on sha256 of provider, model, absolute PDF path and size:mtime - and structurally revalidated on load, so it is the only cache layer that cannot go stale.

nodes.label: Python Dependency Manifest
nodes.rationale: All entries are deliberately unpinned and grouped by comment into Core, LLM/embeddings, Vector index and Tests.

nodes.label: Build-Path Scrubbing and Two-Tier Diagnostics
nodes.rationale: Published pages carry a one-line failure summary with absolute paths replaced by <path>; the unabridged tracebacks go to llm_codegen_failures.txt for the maintainer. Readers never see the build machine's filesystem.

nodes.label: GraphSanitizer with Tarjan SCC Collapse
nodes.rationale: Collapsing strongly connected components means mutually-dependent rules still yield a stable cycle-free ordering, and a recovery heuristic rescues a start node that looks suspiciously dependency-free by checking the reverse map for candidate providers.

nodes.label: Placeholder-Aware Caching and Targeted Regeneration
nodes.rationale: isRetryablePlaceholder and Utils.isRetryableExplanationPlaceholder distinguish a real cached answer from a failure marker, so failures are retried next run while good content is reused for free and only the missing example type is re-billed.

nodes.label: Server-Directed 429 Backoff
nodes.rationale: Parses the gateway's own 'Limit resets at:' timestamp and waits the real interval rather than guessing, handling both plain 429s and ones nested inside a 500 envelope.

nodes.label: CLI reference and flag grammar
nodes.rationale: Only --reportPath is mandatory, and it also roots both LLM cache directories. Toggle flags are switches that flip a default true to false. Flags parse left to right with later ones overriding earlier; any unrecognised flag prints usage and exits 255. The --llm= value grammar originally treated anything not off/false/0 as ON, so --llm=disable silently enabled the feature - now strictly validated.

nodes.label: Graceful Degradation Everywhere
nodes.rationale: Per-rule try/catch during composition, per-language and per-example-type isolation during generation, and RAG failures falling back to no-context generation — a partial failure yields a slightly less rich page, never a broken run.

nodes.label: Three Independent Override Axes with JAR Fallback
nodes.norm_label: three independent override axes with jar fallback
nodes.rationale: --rulesDir (input), --ftlTemplatesPath (HTML structure) and --langTemplatesPath (sentence wording) can each be redirected to disk while the others stay bundled, so the tool is self-contained by default yet fully customisable without a rebuild.

nodes.label: Clean bills of health
nodes.rationale: Checked with nothing found: Utils.leafToRootOrderTopo (Kahn with cycle fallback), Utils.extract, gateway_rate_limit.py's sliding window, locking and atomic state write, the reworked EnsuresCaseTwo break binding, and crysl.ftl / header.ftl. Recorded so they are not re-investigated.

nodes.label: Dual backend - OpenAI and UPB AI-Gateway
nodes.norm_label: dual backend - openai and upb ai-gateway
nodes.rationale: --llm-backend fully determines which is used; no fallback between them occurs. Known asymmetry: llm_writer_gateway.py threads GATEWAY_CHAT_MODEL/GATEWAY_EMB_MODEL into its shared CLI config while llm_writer.py passes neither, so OPENAI_CHAT_MODEL affects the code-example writers but is silently ignored by the explanation writer, which stays hardcoded to gpt-4o-mini.

nodes.label: Cross-process gateway RPM throttle
nodes.rationale: The only concurrency primitive in the repository: a JSON timestamp file guarded by fcntl.flock or msvcrt.locking with an atomic temp-file-rename write. It is correctly built for concurrent callers even though nothing in the pipeline calls it concurrently - it exists because the state file is process-durable, protecting against two separate crysldoc invocations racing.

nodes.label: UPB AI-Gateway backend setup
nodes.rationale: GATEWAY_EMB_MODEL is required for secure example generation because there is no working embedding fallback for the gateway; chat model and base URL do have built-in UPB defaults. Gateway chat and embedding requests are throttled client-side by a shared cross-process limiter defaulting to 10 RPM, and no fallback to OpenAI is performed in gateway mode.

nodes.label: Deliberate absence of a concurrency model
nodes.norm_label: deliberate absence of a concurrency model
nodes.rationale: Zero threads, executors, parallel streams or synchronization in Java; zero threading, asyncio or multiprocessing in Python. Subprocesses are spawned strictly one at a time and blocked on. Landmine for future parallelization: Order.java keeps three static fields as per-rule scratch space cleared in a finally block, safe only because rules are processed sequentially. Idempotency is cache-based, not transactional - a run killed mid-write leaves partial files and a rerun resumes from there.

nodes.label: Explanation-Dominated Phase Split
nodes.rationale: 85.9% of wall-clock went to explanations not because explanations were slow but because the code-example phase was unusually cheap — no rule ever entered a long repair cycle.

nodes.label: compile_java() Gate and Repair Budget
nodes.rationale: Writes to a TemporaryDirectory, runs javac --release with a 20-second timeout, and treats a timeout as an ordinary compile failure rather than a crash so one hung compile cannot abort the run. CRYSLDOC_COMPILE_USE_RUNTIME_CLASSPATH=1 compiles against the project's own tree and deliberately weakens the gate.

nodes.label: llm_code_writer_secure.py — Largest Python Module
nodes.rationale: 1,284 LOC, degree 52 — the most connected Python file; it owns prompt shaping, RAG retrieval, deterministic repair and the javac compile-and-repair loop.

nodes.label: Compile-Verify-Repair Loop
nodes.rationale: Deterministic cleanup runs first so no model call is spent on mistakes a rule can fix; compiler diagnostics are then fed back for up to seven rounds, and if all attempts are exhausted a short explanatory comment is published rather than broken code.

nodes.label: Dependency-Aware Prompting
nodes.rationale: The secure-example prompt walks the rule's dependency chain and pulls in the constraints and guarantees of the classes it depends on, so the model produces a correct multi-object setup sequence rather than a call in isolation.

nodes.label: Insecure Example Intentionally Not Compile-Verified
nodes.rationale: The insecure example exists to illustrate a flawed usage pattern, not to run, so subjecting it to the compile gate would add cost without adding value.

nodes.label: JDK-Only javac Compile Gate
nodes.rationale: Compilation is deliberately run against the JDK alone rather than the project's own dependency tree, so an example that compiles here is guaranteed to compile for a reader who has nothing but a JDK.

nodes.label: Insecure example generation flow
nodes.rationale: Deliberately minimal by contrast with the secure path: a single temperature-0.3 prompt asking the model to violate the rule while staying syntactically valid, with no compile check, no patching and no repair loop. It also interpolates ComposedRule fields including their embedded HTML markup directly into the prompt.

nodes.label: Secure example generation flow
nodes.rationale: The most elaborate feature: a size-shaped authoritative CrySL contract with a drop-priority order, a cached CrySL primer from the paper index, a temperature-0.0 prompt with a strict compilation contract plus 13 lettered security guardrails, deterministic post-patching of known model mistakes, then compile-and-repair for up to CRYSLDOC_MAX_REPAIRS rounds. If still failing it raises rather than emit broken code, and Java records a typed placeholder the next run retries.

nodes.label: A6 - Parameter names string-replaced into diagram labels
nodes.norm_label: a6 - parameter names string-replaced into diagram labels
nodes.rationale: Labels were built with parameter names then each name globally String.replace'd with its type, so single-letter names like p, q, g corrupted the method name and each substitution corrupted the previous one's output. Found while verifying the A1 fix. Fixed by constructing the label directly from structured parameters so no replacement happens and no corruption is possible.

nodes.label: A7 - Generic parameter types truncated at the last dot
nodes.norm_label: a7 - generic parameter types truncated at the last dot
nodes.rationale: substring(lastIndexOf('.')+1) breaks on generics: Set<TrustAnchor> became TrustAnchor> with the outer type lost and a dangling bracket. Fixed with toSimpleTypeName, which shortens every qualified name within the type expression and preserves structure.

nodes.label: B2 - Known-API-mistake rewrite corrupts correct TrustAnchor code
nodes.norm_label: b2 - known-api-mistake rewrite corrupts correct trustanchor code
nodes.rationale: A regex meant to repair a model hallucination fired on any two-identifier TrustAnchor call, silently dropping nameConstraints - a real JDK constructor argument and a PKIX security control - while still failing to repair the case it targeted. Removed entirely with a comment recording why: the compile-and-repair loop already handles hallucinated overloads without the risk of silently editing correct code.

nodes.label: N7 - Substring-based variable-to-method matching yields position -1
nodes.norm_label: n7 - substring-based variable-to-method matching yields position -1
nodes.rationale: Candidate methods were selected with contains(variableName) then the ordinal computed with indexOf on a whitespace-split signature, so a name that prefixes another matches but resolves to -1. Latent - zero -1 values reached any page. Fixed with a shared FunctionUtils.hasParameterNamed across nine call sites in four classes so selection agrees with the position computation that follows it. Zero output change across 51 pages, exactly as predicted for a latent defect.

nodes.label: Shared cognicryptdoc_resources Temp Directory Defect
nodes.rationale: The JAR-resource temp directory is a fixed shared path deleted by whichever JVM exits first, so two instances cannot safely run at the same time regardless of --reportPath.

nodes.label: Tier 2 — Python LLM Sidecar
nodes.rationale: Java spawns a Python process per enrichment request; content returns over stdout and diagnostics over stderr, kept separate so diagnostics can never leak into published documentation.

nodes.label: CrySLReader.getOrCreateTempDir Concurrency Defect
nodes.rationale: It resolves a fixed path ${java.io.tmpdir}/cognicryptdoc_resources identical for every JVM and registers it with deleteOnExit(); when the concurrent job exited, its shutdown hooks deleted the directory out from under a still-running job and the atomic move of frontpage.ftl failed with NoSuchFileException. The temp directory is not scoped per run.

nodes.label: Placeholder-Aware Per-Rule Caching
nodes.rationale: The cache distinguishes a real answer from a failure placeholder, so a failed generation is retried automatically on the next run while everything that already succeeded is reused for free.

nodes.label: Cache-Based Run Recovery with --llm=off
nodes.rationale: Re-running with --llm=off against the same --reportPath reused every cached explanation and example, made no API calls, and rendered all 51 pages in 1.4 s — the crashed run's site was recovered without repeating two hours of model work, with cache contents verified byte-for-byte against a pre-recovery backup.

nodes.label: Placeholder-Aware Self-Healing Cache
nodes.rationale: isRetryablePlaceholder() and Utils.isRetryableExplanationPlaceholder() recognise failure markers such as '// LLM secure example failed:' and 'disabled by flag.', so a failed run self-heals: re-running regenerates only what failed and real content is reused for free.

nodes.label: Empty-Completion Failure Mode
nodes.rationale: o4-mini returns a completion with no content, so the compile gate is never reached and the repair loop never engages — a categorically different and more serious failure than Qwen3-30B and gpt-4o-mini, which at least produced code that could be checked and repaired.

nodes.label: max_tokens Budget Exhaustion Hypothesis
nodes.rationale: The secure path sends max_tokens=2000 with a large system message while the insecure path sends no max_tokens at all, and o4-mini spends 1,024–1,216 tokens on hidden reasoning before emitting visible output — but isolated reproduction attempts returned working code every time, so the correlation is stated as an open question and no causal claim is made.

nodes.label: Misleadingly Cheap Example Phase
nodes.rationale: The code-example phase looks cheap per rule only because most secure examples failed outright and never entered the compile-repair loop; a better-performing model would spend more time in this phase, not less.

nodes.label: Failure Reproduced Under Clean Conditions
nodes.rationale: 48 empty completions in each of two runs, one concurrent and one solo — an almost exact reproduction that rules out the measurement conditions as the cause and establishes the failure as a property of the model on this workload.

nodes.label: Cross-Backend Quality Comparison Table
nodes.rationale: gpt-5.4-mini 51/51, gpt-4o-mini 49/51, qwen3-30b 39/51, o4-mini 11/51 on an identical 51-rule set; wall-clock comparisons are indicative only because some runs were measured under concurrency.

nodes.label: gpt-5.4-mini Gateway Runtime Result
nodes.rationale: 4,630 s solo for 51 rules vs 1.28 s with --llm=off; 51/51 secure and 51/51 insecure examples across two runs with zero 429s. The run was repeated because LLM output is non-deterministic and a repeat was the only way to show the perfect compile-gate score was a property of the model rather than a lucky draw.

nodes.label: o4-mini Gateway Runtime Result
nodes.rationale: 5,236 s solo for 51 rules; explanations largely succeeded (193/204) but only 14/51 secure examples were produced at all. The decisive result is quality, not speed, which makes the model unsuitable for the code-example feature as currently configured.

nodes.label: FAISS RAG Grounding on the CrySL Paper
nodes.norm_label: faiss rag grounding on the crysl paper
nodes.rationale: Two distinct grounding mechanisms draw on the same indexed paper: a cached primer that teaches the DSL's semantics once, and per-rule retrieval that pulls passages specific to the class being documented.

nodes.label: Priority-Truncated CrySL Contract Shaping
nodes.rationale: When the prompt runs long, ORDER and FORBIDDEN are preserved longest while ENSURES/CONSTRAINTS are trimmed first, because call order and forbidden methods are the parts the generated example cannot get wrong.

nodes.label: FAISS RAG Grounding on the CrySL Paper
nodes.norm_label: faiss rag grounding on the crysl paper

nodes.label: CDN Browser Assets Without Local Fallback
nodes.norm_label: cdn browser assets without local fallback
nodes.rationale: d3, d3-graphviz, @hpcc-js/wasm and marked are hardcoded CDN loads in singleclass.ftl with no vendored copy, so offline the diagrams and Markdown rendering degrade while static text still renders.

nodes.label: Generated Static Site as the Frontend
nodes.norm_label: generated static site as the frontend
nodes.rationale: No React, Vue, Angular, bundler or package.json — the frontend is the generated frameset site with ten plain JavaScript functions and DOM-only state, self-contained enough to open over file:// or serve from any static host.

nodes.label: Finding 3 — The Two Backends Genuinely Share a Core
nodes.norm_label: finding 3 — the two backends genuinely share a core
nodes.rationale: llm_writer.py and llm_writer_gateway.py both import process_rule_core, run_writer_main, build_explanation_prompt, build_system_messages, extract_completion_text and WriterCLIConfig from writer_core — the shared abstraction is real, not aspirational.

nodes.label: writer_core Template Method Shared by Both Backends
nodes.norm_label: writer_core template method shared by both backends
nodes.rationale: run_writer_main() lets backends inject init_client_fn, build_pdf_index_fn and process_rule_fn; both llm_writer.py and llm_writer_gateway.py import the same six symbols, so the abstraction is real rather than aspirational. build_system_messages() returns a single system message because the UPB gateway rejects a second one.
